q: Oxygen is the most abundant element in the Earth’s crust. The free element accounts for ____ of the volume of the atmosphere.
e: This percentage indicates the proportion of oxygen in the atmosphere, essential for respiration.

q: Oxygen in the combined state exists in water, sand or silica, silicates and ____ .
e: Rocks are natural solid aggregates of minerals and can contain oxygen in various forms.

q: Oxygen preparation can be demonstrated in a number of ways in the classroom or in the ____ .
e: The laboratory setting allows for controlled experiments to demonstrate chemical reactions.

q: Potassium chlorate should not be used for the preparation of oxygen in the laboratory due to its ____ nature.
e: Toxic substances can pose health risks if inhaled or ingested.

q: In the laboratory or in the classroom, oxygen gas can be prepared by using an environmentally friendly liquid ____ of appropriate strength.
e: Hydrogen peroxide is a common reagent used to generate oxygen gas safely.

q: In this reaction, manganese(IV) oxide is used as a ____ to speed up the chemical reaction.
e: A catalyst increases the rate of a chemical reaction without being consumed in the process.

q: Oxygen gas is collected by the downward displacement of ____ .
e: This method utilizes the property of gases being less dense than liquids to collect gas.

q: Oxygen is a colourless gas, without taste or smell. Oxygen is only slightly soluble in ____ .
e: Solubility in water affects how oxygen is available for aquatic life.

q: Oxygen will not burn; however, it supports ____ .
e: Combustion is the chemical process of burning that requires oxygen.

q: If rekindles any glowing thing (splinter) with a bright flame, it indicates the presence of ____ .
e: The rekindling of a splinter shows that oxygen supports combustion.

q: Metals such as magnesium, iron, copper and zinc react with oxygen forming ____ .
e: Oxides are compounds formed when elements react with oxygen.

q: A piece of clean magnesium ribbon continues burning in oxygen from air with a dazzling white flame, leaving a white powder as ____ .
e: Residue is the solid left after a reaction, in this case, magnesium oxide.

q: This residue is magnesium oxide: magnesium + oxygen -> ____ .
e: Magnesium oxide is the product of the reaction between magnesium and oxygen.

q: Iron slowly becomes oxidised in the presence of air and water, to form hydrated iron(II) oxide, i.e., iron has become ____ .
e: Rusting is the corrosion of iron caused by oxidation.

q: Most useful metals or sheets become covered with thin films of metal ____ .
e: Metal oxides can protect metals from further corrosion.

q: Non-metals such as phosphorus, sulphur and carbon react with oxygen to form ____ .
e: Non-metal oxides are products of reactions between non-metals and oxygen.

q: A small piece of phosphorus burns in oxygen giving off white fumes which consist of oxides of ____ .
e: Phosphorus oxides are formed when phosphorus reacts with oxygen.

q: Phosphorus + oxygen -> ____ .
e: Phosphorus(V) oxide is formed in this reaction.

q: Phosphorus + oxygen -> ____ .
e: Phosphorus(III) oxide is another product of phosphorus reacting with oxygen.

q: An oxide is a compound containing ____ and another element.
e: Oxygen is a key element in oxides, which can form with various other elements.

q: An acidic oxide is an oxide of ____ .
e: Acidic oxides typically come from non-metallic elements.

q: Acidic oxides react with basic oxides to give ____ only.
e: Salts are the products of neutralization reactions between acids and bases.

q: Some acidic oxides are soluble in water but some are not. CO2, SO2, SO3 and P2O5 are soluble oxides while SiO2 is an ____ oxide.
e: Insoluble oxides do not dissolve in water to form acidic solutions.

q: Soluble acidic oxides dissolve in water to form acidic solutions. These solutions turn blue litmus ____ .
e: Litmus paper changes color in response to acidity.

q: Sulphur trioxide + water -> ____ .
e: Sulphuric acid is formed from the reaction of sulphur trioxide with water.

q: A basic oxide is an oxide of ____ .
e: Basic oxides are derived from metallic elements.

q: A basic oxide reacts with an acid to produce a ____ and water only.
e: The reaction between an acid and a base produces salt and water.

q: A basic oxide neutralises ____ .
e: Basic oxides react with acids to form salts.

q: Some basic oxides are soluble in water but some are not. Na2O and K2O are soluble oxides while MgO, CuO and Ag2O are ____ .
e: These oxides do not dissolve in water to form alkaline solutions.

q: Some basic oxides react with water forming ____ solutions (alkalis).
e: Hydroxide solutions are alkaline and turn red litmus blue.

q: Sodium oxide + water -> ____ .
e: Sodium hydroxide is formed when sodium oxide reacts with water.

q: An amphoteric oxide is a metallic oxide which possesses both, basic and ____ properties.
e: Amphoteric oxides can react with both acids and bases.

q: An amphoteric oxide reacts with both acids and alkalis to form ____ and water.
e: The reaction with acids and bases produces salt and water.

q: Zinc oxide + sulphuric acid (dil.) -> ____ .
e: Zinc sulphate is formed from the reaction of zinc oxide with sulphuric acid.

q: Zinc oxide + sodium hydroxide -> ____ .
e: Sodium zincate is produced when zinc oxide reacts with sodium hydroxide.

q: The neutral oxide is an oxide which shows neither basic nor ____ character.
e: Neutral oxides do not exhibit the properties of acids or bases.

q: Those oxides that react with an acid to give salt and hydrogen peroxide are called ____ .
e: Peroxides release hydrogen peroxide when reacting with acids.

q: A compound oxide is an oxide, formed by the combination of two different oxides of the same ____ .
e: Compound oxides consist of two oxides of the same element.

q: PbO2 is a compound oxide consisting of lead(II) and lead(IV) oxides. It can be written as di-lead(II) lead(IV) oxide or ____ lead oxide.
e: Red lead oxide is a well-known compound oxide.

q: When red lead oxide reacts with dilute nitric acid, lead(II) oxide only reacts with the acid to form lead(II) ____ .
e: Lead(II) nitrate is produced from the reaction with nitric acid.

q: Oxygen is used to help patients with ____ difficulties.
e: Breathing difficulties can be alleviated with supplemental oxygen.

q: In aquatic habitat, organisms use oxygen dissolved in ____ .
e: Aquatic organisms rely on dissolved oxygen for respiration.

q: In living organisms, the oxygen intake is used for the breakdown of the glucose molecules to produce ____ .
e: Energy is produced through cellular respiration using oxygen.

q: Oxygen is used in steel work, and oxyacetylene gas mixture is used for ____ and welding metals.
e: Cutting metals requires high temperatures generated by oxyacetylene flames.

q: Liquid oxygen is carried on rockets to support the fuel ____ .
e: Liquid oxygen is essential for combustion in rocket engines.

q: Usefulness of some oxides in society includes their role as bleaching agents, pigments used in paints, and in cement ____ .
e: Oxides play various roles in industrial applications.

q: Carbon is found in nature as ____ and graphite.
e: Diamond is one of the allotropes of carbon, known for its hardness.

q: Carbon can also be found as compounds combining with other elements in petroleum, coal, natural gas, limestone, carbon dioxide and ____ .
e: Sugar is an organic compound that contains carbon.

q: If an element can exist in more than one form, in the same physical state, it is said to exhibit ____ or polymorphism.
e: Allotropy refers to the existence of an element in different forms.

q: The different forms of an element in the same physical state that possess different physical properties are known as ____ of that element.
e: Allotropes have distinct physical and sometimes chemical properties.

q: Diamond, graphite, fullerene and graphene are ____ of carbon.
e: These are different structural forms of carbon.

q: In diamond, each carbon atom is surrounded by ____ other carbon atoms.
e: This tetrahedral arrangement contributes to diamond's strength.

q: Diamond has a giant structure containing millions of carbon atoms in a three dimensional network of strong carbon-carbon ____ .
e: Covalent bonds are strong connections between atoms.

q: Diamond is very hard and has a very high melting point of ____ °C.
e: This high melting point is due to the strong covalent bonds in diamond.

q: Graphite is soft due to its layered structure where each carbon atom is surrounded by ____ other carbon atoms in the same plane.
e: This planar arrangement allows layers to slide over each other.

q: Graphite has a soapy touch and can act as a ____ due to its layered structure.
e: Graphite's layered structure allows it to reduce friction.

q: Graphite is a good conductor of electricity and heat due to the presence of ____ electrons.
e: Free electrons allow graphite to conduct electricity.

q: The melting point of graphite is ____ °C.
e: Graphite has a high melting point due to strong covalent bonds.

q: Fullerene (C60) is an allotrope of carbon in the form of a hollow sphere, ellipsoid, tube and many other shapes and sizes. Spherical fullerenes are also referred to as ____ balls.
e: Bucky balls are a specific type of fullerene.

q: Graphene is a single layer (monolayer) of graphite and is tightly bound in a ____ ring structure.
e: Hexagonal arrangements are characteristic of graphene's structure.

q: Graphene is about ____ times stronger than the strongest steel.
e: Graphene's strength-to-weight ratio is exceptionally high.

q: Graphene is a transparent and flexible conductor widely used for various material/device applications, including solar cells, light-emitting diodes (LED), touch panels and ____ windows or phones.
e: Smart devices utilize graphene for its conductive properties.

q: Charcoal is made by heating wood in the absence of ____ .
e: This process prevents combustion and results in charcoal.

q: Coal is found in nature and is a black heavy ____ .
e: Coal is a naturally occurring fossil fuel.

q: Coke is formed by heating coal in the absence of ____ .
e: Coke is a purer form of carbon used in various applications.

q: Carbon black (soot) is a black powder formed when kerosene is burnt in a limited amount of ____ .
e: Limited air supply leads to incomplete combustion, producing soot.

q: When carbon burns in excess air or oxygen, carbon dioxide is formed. Carbon monoxide is formed when carbon burns in a ____ amount of air or oxygen.
e: Limited oxygen leads to incomplete combustion, producing carbon monoxide.

q: Carbon can be used as a reducing agent in the extraction of some metals. When strongly heated, carbon can reduce the oxides of zinc and other metals such as CuO, PbO and ____ to their respective metals.
e: Iron(III) oxide can be reduced by carbon to produce iron.

q: Carbon + oxygen (excess) -> ____ .
e: This reaction represents complete combustion of carbon.

q: Carbon + oxygen (limited) -> ____ .
e: This reaction represents incomplete combustion of carbon.

q: Halogens (F2, Cl2, Br2, I2) are diatomic molecules. More reactive ____ is the most reactive.
e: Fluorine is the most electronegative and reactive of all elements.

q: Fluorine and chlorine are gases, bromine is a ____ and iodine is a solid at room temperature.
e: Bromine is the only liquid halogen at room temperature.

q: Halogens are highly electronegative elements. Since the essential electronic structure of halogen is ns2 np5, they are very ____ .
e: High reactivity is due to their tendency to gain electrons.

q: None of the halogens can be found in nature in their elemental forms. They are found as salts of the ____ .
e: Halides are compounds formed from halogens and metals.

q: In the laboratory, halogen is prepared by heating sodium or potassium halide with manganese(IV) oxide and concentrated ____ acid.
e: Concentrated sulphuric acid is used to produce halogens.

q: Chlorine is prepared from the mixture of sodium chloride, manganese(IV) oxide and concentrated sulphuric acid on heating. It is collected by the upward displacement of ____ .
e: Chlorine is less soluble in water and heavier than air.

q: Fluorine is a very pale yellow gas. It is the lightest halogen and exists as a highly ____ gas.
e: Fluorine's toxicity makes it dangerous to handle.

q: Chlorine is a pale green gas with a choking, unpleasant smell. Chlorine is very poisonous if inhaled even in ____ quantities.
e: Even small amounts of chlorine can be harmful.

q: Bromine is a heavy, reddish brown, volatile liquid. It has a choking, irritating smell. Liquid bromine causes ____ on the flesh.
e: Bromine can cause severe skin irritation and burns.

q: Iodine is a purple-black shiny solid with an irritating smell. Iodine sublimes rapidly when heated, forming a violet ____ .
e: Sublimation is the transition from solid to gas without passing through a liquid phase.

q: Halogens react with most compounds containing ____ .
e: Halogens readily react with hydrogen to form hydrogen halides.

q: When a tube containing equal volumes of chlorine and hydrogen is exposed to sunlight, it ____ .
e: This reaction is highly exothermic and produces hydrogen chloride.

q: Chlorine reacts vigorously with metals to form metal ____ .
e: Metal chlorides are formed through direct reactions with metals.

q: Iron + chlorine -> ____ .
e: Iron(II) chloride is formed when iron reacts with chlorine.

q: Copper + chlorine -> ____ .
e: Copper(II) chloride is produced from the reaction of copper with chlorine.

q: Bromine combines readily with most metals to form ____ .
e: Bromides are the products of reactions between bromine and metals.

q: Phosphorus burns spontaneously in chlorine to form ____ .
e: Phosphorus(III) chloride is formed from the reaction of phosphorus with chlorine.

q: Chlorine reacts with water to form hypochlorous acid and ____ acid.
e: This reaction produces two acids from chlorine and water.

q: The HOCI slowly decomposes to nascent ____ .
e: Nascent oxygen is highly reactive and can bleach substances.

q: Chlorine will bleach moist litmus papers. This is used as a test for ____ .
e: Bleaching indicates the presence of chlorine gas.

q: Halides are formed when halogens combine with ____ .
e: Halides are ionic compounds formed from halogens and metals.

q: The presence of chloride, bromide or iodide ions can be tested by adding ____ nitrate solution.
e: Silver nitrate is used to detect halide ions by forming precipitates.
